title: Search strategies, local search and limits

questions.heading: Stop on Solutions, Not Seconds, When a Result Must Repeat
questions.stem: A routing report uses PATH_CHEAPEST_ARC, guided local search and a 20-second time limit. A colleague on a faster laptop gets other routes from the same data. What makes the two runs agree?

options.text: Fix the strategy and stop on a solution count, not on seconds
options.says: Right: a solution limit makes the search's end independent of the machine's speed.

options.text: Raise the time limit to 120 seconds, so both reach the same optimum
options.says: More seconds still stop at a machine-dependent point, and the search proves no optimum.

options.text: Switch to AUTOMATIC, so the solver always picks the same strategy
options.says: The strategy was never the problem; the time limit is what differs between machines.

options.text: Use an lns_time_limit instead, so every move gets the same seconds
options.says: lns_time_limit is still wall time, per move; any time limit makes where the search stops depend on the machine.

questions.heading: The Status Says Whether You Have Routes, Not Whether They Are Optimal
questions.stem: A planner's run ends with routing.status() returning ROUTING_SUCCESS and a plan of 412 drive minutes. What does the status tell the planner?

options.text: That 412 is optimal, since a heuristic run would report a partial success
options.says: Greedy descent reported SUCCESS for plans from 253 to 287 on one model; SUCCESS is not optimality.

options.text: That 412 is within 1% of optimal, the routing library's default gap
options.says: The routing library computes no bound, so it has no gap at all.

options.text: That some visits were dropped, since a full plan would report OPTIMAL
options.says: The status says nothing about drops; dropped visits are read from the successors.

options.text: That routes were found and the search ended normally, nothing more
options.says: Right: SUCCESS means routes and a normal end; no proof of optimality.

questions.heading: Local Search Improves Them, and a Metaheuristic Escapes Local Minima
questions.stem: With greedy descent, a model's runs from four first-solution strategies end at 610, 598, 610 and 587 minutes. Why do they not all end at the same cost?

options.text: The solver has a bug, since local search always ends at the optimum
options.says: Local search ends at a local minimum, which need not be the optimum.

options.text: Each start descends to its own local minimum, where no move helps
options.says: Right: the lesson's table shows each strategy's greedy descent ending between 253 and 287.

options.text: Greedy descent stops on a clock, so slower strategies get less search
options.says: Greedy descent stops when no move improves the plan, not on a clock.

options.text: The strategies build different models, so their optimal costs differ
options.says: The model is the same; only the starting routes differ.
